Department: Rheumatology
Mode of Admission: Planned
Complaints: Pain in hip joints (predominantly left); Periodic pain in wrists, cervical, and thoracic spine
History of Present Illness: Patient has been ill since the age of 12. Disease began acutely after an episode of tonsillitis. Fever and swelling of the ankle joint were noted. Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA) was not diagnosed initially. Antibiotic therapy was ineffective. Condition improved after IV corticosteroids. Later, high-dose methylprednisolone therapy led to systemic osteoporosis. Methotrexate was added. Since 2014, on tocilizumab (Actemra) with clinical improvement.
Current Treatment: Tocilizumab 162 mg SC every 2 weeks (state program); Methotrexate 10 mg weekly; Folic acid 5 mg; Calcium supplements; Alendronate; NSAIDs as needed (almost daily)
Objective Exam General Condition: moderate severity
Objective Examination Details: Consciousness: clear; Skin/mucosa: normal color, clean, moderately moist; Lymph nodes: not palpable; Lungs: vesicular breath sounds throughout; Heart: rhythmic activity, clear tones; Abdomen: symmetrical, soft, non-tender; Liver/Spleen: not palpable; Pasternatsky symptom: negative bilaterally; Bowel/bladder: within normal limits
Local Status: Multiple striae on abdomen, thighs, arms
Primary Diagnosis: Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis
Complications of Primary Diagnosis: Systemic osteoporosis (due to therapy)
Additional Diagnoses/Conditions from Unnamed Column: Tonsillitis (precipitating illness)

Patient Initials: V.
Gender: Female
DOB: Not provided
Age: 27
Date of Admission: Not provided
Department: Allergy/Immunology
Mode of Admission: Not provided
Complaints: Episodes of urticaria; Lip swelling; Stomach pain after consuming strawberries, peaches, apples, and kiwi
History of Present Illness: Female, 27 years old, resident of Khmelnytskyi region, Ukraine. Symptoms began two years ago. No previous history of allergic diseases. Initially examined by an allergist and tested for respiratory allergens – results were negative for specific IgE. Frequency of episodes: 1–2 times per month. Manifestations: urticaria, lip swelling, abdominal pain. Good response to antihistamines. Referred for extended allergological testing (ALEX test). Test Results: Positive specific IgE to nsLTP (non-specific lipid transfer proteins) found in peanuts, kiwi, peaches, and apples. Interpretation: nsLTP syndrome is commonly found in the Mediterranean region. The patient has never visited this region. Conclusion: nsLTP syndrome may occur outside the Mediterranean, likely due to sensitization from kiwi consumption.
Current Treatment: Antihistamines as needed
Objective Exam General Condition: Not provided
Objective Examination Details: Not provided
Local Status: Not provided
Primary Diagnosis: nsLTP syndrome; Recurrent allergic urticaria and angioedema (Quincke's edema); Oral allergy syndrome without pollen allergy; Food allergy
Complications of Primary Diagnosis: Not provided
Additional Diagnoses/Conditions from Unnamed Column: Not provided
Course Summary: Not provided

case:
Patient: Girl, 5 years old
Chief Complaint: Rash and itching on the face, buttocks, and limbs
History:
Symptoms began two weeks ago, 8–10 days after a non-specified viral infection. No previous history of allergic diseases.
Course of Illness:
The rash remained stable for 10 days and did not respond to antihistamines.
Physical Examination:
The rash is mixed in character: flesh-colored papules (2–4 mm) present either on unaffected skin or against an erythematous background. Distribution: face, buttocks, extensor surfaces of both upper and lower limbs. Body temperature is normal. Lymph nodes are not enlarged. General condition is unaffected.
Diagnosis: Gianotti-Crosti syndrome (papular acrodermatitis, viral exanthem)
Follow-up: Parents declined further investigations. Full recovery occurred two weeks after presentation (i.e., four weeks after rash onset).
